title: A finite type domain over a field has the dimension of each of its local rings at maximal ideals
statement: Let $k$ be a field and $S$ a finite type $k$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra] which is an integral domain. Then for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\subset S$ the Krull dimension [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring] of the localization $S_{\mathfrak m}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] equals the Krull dimension of $S$: $\dim(S_{\mathfrak m})=\dim(S)$, and this is a non-negative integer. Equivalently, every maximal chain of prime ideals of $S$ (a chain $\mathfrak q_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak q_t$ of prime ideals that cannot be lengthened by inserting a prime ideal before $\mathfrak q_0$, between two consecutive members, or after $\mathfrak q_t$) has length $t=\dim(S)$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00OS (label lemma-dimension-spell-it-out, line 27763); its proof uses Proposition 00OQ (proposition-finite-gl-dim-polynomial-ring) and Lemma 00OR (lemma-dimension-height-polynomial-ring); tags verified in stacks-project/tags/tags

proof.text: (Setup.) As $S$ is a finite type $k$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra] there are $n\ge0$ and a surjective $k$-algebra map $\pi:P=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]\to S$ from the polynomial ring [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. Let $\mathfrak p=\ker\pi$; since $P/\mathfrak p\cong S$ is an integral domain, $\mathfrak p$ is a prime ideal of $P$. Correspondence of ideals: $Q\mapsto\pi(Q)$ and $\mathfrak q\mapsto\pi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$ are mutually inverse inclusion-preserving bijections between the ideals of $P$ containing $\mathfrak p$ and the ideals of $S$, and $P/Q\cong S/\pi(Q)$, so $Q$ is prime (resp. maximal) iff $\pi(Q)$ is. In particular a chain of primes $\mathfrak q_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak q_t$ of $S$ gives the chain $\pi^{-1}(\mathfrak q_0)\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\pi^{-1}(\mathfrak q_t)$ of primes of $P$ of the same length, all containing $\mathfrak p$. Since $S$ is a domain, $S\neq0$ and $(0)$ is a prime ideal of $S$, contained in every prime ideal of $S$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 00OS (lemma-dimension-spell-it-out, line 27763), proof, first sentence 'Write S = k[x_1, ..., x_n]/p'

proof.text: (Bounds.) Every chain $Q_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq Q_t$ of prime ideals of $P$ has $t\le n$: $Q_t\neq P$, so $Q_t\subseteq M$ for a maximal ideal $M$ of $P$ [lem-weil-pbc-proper-ideal-contained-in-maximal]; by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-dimension-chains-below-prime] $t\le\dim(P_M)$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime, def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring], and $\dim(P_M)=n$ by [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-ring-maximal-localization-dimension]. By step 1 every chain of prime ideals of $S$ therefore has length $\le n$; in particular $0\le\dim S\le n$ ($S$ has the prime $(0)$), and for each prime $\mathfrak q$ of $S$ the lengths of the chains of primes of $S$ ending inside $\mathfrak q$ are bounded by $n$.

source.place: Algebra, Proposition 00OQ (proposition-finite-gl-dim-polynomial-ring, line 27723: the localizations at maximal ideals have dimension n), via Lemma 00OP (lemma-dim-affine-space, line 27660), as used in the proof of Lemma 00OS

proof.text: (Height of a maximal ideal of $P$.) Let $\operatorname{ht}$ be the height of [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-ring-maximal-chain-height-difference]: the supremum of the lengths of chains of primes of $P$ ending inside the given prime. For a maximal ideal $M$ of $P$, [lem-weil-pbc-localization-dimension-chains-below-prime] says that this supremum is $\dim(P_M)$, which is $n$ by [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-ring-maximal-localization-dimension]: $\operatorname{ht}(M)=n$. Also $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)\le n$ is an integer by [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-ring-maximal-chain-height-difference].

source.place: Algebra, Proposition 00OQ (line 27723) and Lemma 00OR (line 27737), as used in the proof of Lemma 00OS

proof.text: ($\dim(S_{\mathfrak m})=n-\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)$ for every maximal $\mathfrak m$.) Let $\mathfrak m\subset S$ be maximal and $M=\pi^{-1}(\mathfrak m)$, a maximal ideal of $P$ containing $\mathfrak p$ (step 1). By [lem-weil-pbc-localization-dimension-chains-below-prime], $\dim(S_{\mathfrak m})$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime, def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring] is the supremum of the lengths of chains of primes of $S$ ending inside $\mathfrak m$; these lengths are bounded by $n$ (step 2) and the chain $\mathfrak m$ of length $0$ is one of them, so the supremum $d=\dim(S_{\mathfrak m})$ is attained by a chain $C:\mathfrak q_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak q_d\subseteq\mathfrak m$. Because no such chain is longer than $C$: $\mathfrak q_0=(0)$ (otherwise prepend the prime $(0)\subsetneq\mathfrak q_0$, step 1); $\mathfrak q_d=\mathfrak m$ (otherwise append $\mathfrak m$); and no prime $\mathfrak r$ of $S$ satisfies $\mathfrak q_{i-1}\subsetneq\mathfrak r\subsetneq\mathfrak q_i$ (otherwise insert it). Put $Q_i=\pi^{-1}(\mathfrak q_i)$. Then $\mathfrak p=Q_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq Q_d=M$ is a chain of primes of $P$, and no prime $R'$ of $P$ satisfies $Q_{i-1}\subsetneq R'\subsetneq Q_i$: such an $R'$ contains $\mathfrak p$, and $\pi(R')$ would be a prime of $S$ strictly between $\mathfrak q_{i-1}$ and $\mathfrak q_i$ (step 1). So it is a maximal chain of primes between $\mathfrak p$ and $M$, and by [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-ring-maximal-chain-height-difference] and step 3, $d=\operatorname{ht}(M)-\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)=n-\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)$. In particular $\dim(S_{\mathfrak m})=n-\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)$ does not depend on $\mathfrak m$, and $S$ has a chain of primes of this length.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 00OS (line 27763), proof: 'all the maximal chains of primes in S (which necessarily end with a maximal ideal) have length n - height(p). Thus this number is ... the dimension of S_m'

proof.text: ($\dim S=\dim(S_{\mathfrak m})$.) $S\neq0$, so $S$ has a maximal ideal [lem-weil-pbc-proper-ideal-contained-in-maximal], and by step 4 $S$ has a chain of primes of length $n-\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)$; hence $\dim S\ge n-\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)$ [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. Conversely let $\mathfrak q_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak q_t$ be any chain of primes of $S$. The prime $\mathfrak q_t$ lies in a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m'$ [lem-weil-pbc-proper-ideal-contained-in-maximal], so $t\le\dim(S_{\mathfrak m'})$ by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-dimension-chains-below-prime], and $\dim(S_{\mathfrak m'})=n-\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)$ by step 4. Thus $\dim S=n-\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)$, a non-negative integer, and $\dim(S_{\mathfrak m})=\dim S$ for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $S$ by step 4.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 00OS (line 27763), proof, last sentence 'Thus this number is the dimension of S and of S_m for any maximal ideal m of S'

proof.text: (Maximal chains.) Let $\mathfrak q_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak q_t$ be a maximal chain of primes of $S$ in the sense of the statement. Then $\mathfrak q_0=(0)$ (else prepend $(0)$, step 1); $\mathfrak q_t$ is a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ (it lies in a maximal ideal [lem-weil-pbc-proper-ideal-contained-in-maximal], which would otherwise be appended); and no prime lies strictly between consecutive members. As in step 4, the preimages $\pi^{-1}(\mathfrak q_i)$ form a maximal chain of primes of $P$ between $\mathfrak p$ and the maximal ideal $M=\pi^{-1}(\mathfrak m)$, so $t=\operatorname{ht}(M)-\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)=n-\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)=\dim S$ by [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-ring-maximal-chain-height-difference], step 3 and step 5. Conversely, if every maximal chain has length $\dim S$, then for a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ the chain of step 4 is maximal and has length $\dim(S_{\mathfrak m})$, giving $\dim(S_{\mathfrak m})=\dim S$; so the two formulations are equivalent.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 00OS (line 27763), statement 'In words: every maximal chain of primes has length equal to the dimension of S', and proof

split_report.summary: Split following Stacks Algebra 00OS (algebra.tex line 27763), tags 00OS/00OQ/00OR/00OP verified in tags/tags. Mathlib has no statement that every maximal ideal of a finite type domain over a field has height dim S (only Ideal.exists_isMaximal_height: some maximal ideal), nor catenarity; the source repository has none either. Proof: S = k[x_1..x_n]/p (step 1, correspondence of primes); chains of P have length <= n via dim P_M = n (00OP/00OQ, existing node) (step 2); ht(M) = n (step 3); a longest chain below m is saturated from (0) to m, its preimage a maximal chain from p to M, so dim S_m = n - ht(p) by 00OR (new unsplit node) (step 4); dim S = n - ht(p) (step 5); the maximal-chain formulation (step 6). New nodes: lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-ring-maximal-chain-height-difference (00OR, unsplit) and lem-weil-pbc-proper-ideal-contained-in-maximal (00E0, Mathlib leaf Ideal.exists_le_maximal). Statement unchanged in substance; clarified 'maximal chain' and that the dimension is a non-negative integer.

reviewed: pass (L, 2026-10-10): 6 steps follow 00OS: chains in P = k[x] have length <= n (00OP/00OQ localization dimension, new leaf for maximal ideals), ht(M) = n, every maximal chain from p to M has length n - ht(p) (00OR, new unsplit node), so dim S_m = n - ht(p) = dim S. Statement wording clarified only.

lean.statement: theorem finiteTypeDomain_ringKrullDim_localizationAtMaximal {k : Type u} [Field k] {S : Type v} [CommRing S] [Algebra k S] [Algebra.FiniteType k S] [IsDomain S] : (∀ (m : Ideal S) [m.IsMaximal], ringKrullDim (Localization.AtPrime m) = ringKrullDim S) ∧ (∃ (d : ℕ), ringKrullDim S = (d : WithBot ℕ∞) ∧ ∀ (p : LTSeries (PrimeSpectrum S)), IsMaxChain (fun q r : PrimeSpectrum S ↦ q ≤ r) (Set.range p) → p.length = d)
